THOUGHT: This is an elderly, immunosuppressed man (CLL on cyclosporine) who had a viral respiratory prodrome followed by pruritic blisters on the hands/feet that then became widespread with fever and dusky bullae. Key diagnostic data: HSV/VZV PCR negative, Tzanck negative, skin lesion and blood enterovirus PCR positive (strong evidence of systemic enteroviral infection), punch biopsy showing superficial epidermal dyskeratosis/necrosis with mixed inflammation, and direct immunofluorescence negative (argues against Ig-mediated autoimmune blistering). The clinical distribution (initial acral involvement of palms/soles and hands/feet), the progression to more widespread macules/vesicles/bullae in an adult, and systemic viremia strongly favor a severe/disseminated enteroviral hand‑foot‑and‑mouth–type eruption (eg, coxsackie/enterovirus, including A6 variants or “eczema coxsackium”). Important alternatives are drug‑induced mucocutaneous necrolysis (SJS/TEN) given recent antibiotics and epidermal necrosis on biopsy, erythema multiforme, other drug‑related bullous eruptions, and autoimmune subepidermal bullous disease — but these are less likely given enterovirus detection and negative DIF.

DIAGNOSIS:
1. Disseminated enteroviral infection causing severe/bullous hand‑foot‑and‑mouth–type eruption (eg, coxsackie/enterovirus A, including A6/eczema coxsackium) — most likely given positive enterovirus PCR from lesions and blood, acral onset with subsequent widespread bullae, and compatible histology.
2. Stevens‑Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis (drug‑induced mucocutaneous necrolysis) — important close alternative because of recent antibiotics and epidermal necrosis on biopsy, though less likely due to enterovirus viremia and limited mucosal involvement and negative DIF.
3. Erythema multiforme (major) — targetoid/interface process often post‑infectious (classically HSV or Mycoplasma) that can cause mucosal lesions and epidermal necrosis; considered because of necrotic keratinocytes and acute onset but HSV PCR negative and enterovirus positive.
4. Drug‑related bullous eruption (eg, generalized fixed drug eruption or other non‑SJS bullous drug reaction) — possible given recent antibiotics and immunosuppression, but histology/DIF and enterovirus detection make this less likely.
5. Autoimmune subepidermal bullous disease (eg, bullous pemphigoid) — considered because of age and bullae, but DIF is negative and histology lacks the classic subepidermal blister with eosinophils, making this less likely.

Make a diagnosis for the patient's disease based on the case information, physical examination, and diagnostic tests. Enumerate the top 5 most likely diagnoses for the following patient in order, with the most likely disease listed first.

Case Information:
A man in his 70s with a history of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and prescribed cyclosporine, 100 mg twice daily, for pure red cell aplasia. Initial symptoms included rhinorrhea, cough, and low-grade fever 2 weeks prior. After treatment with azithromycin, he developed small, pruritic blisters on hands and feet. Following doxycycline and diphenhydramine prescription at urgent care, he developed worsening fever, chills, and spreading blisters and bullae on arms, legs, and face.

Physical Examination:
Numerous pink to violaceous macules, papules, and patches on the palms, dorsal hands, forearms, elbows, feet, and distal lower extremities. Scattered macules on face, neck, trunk, upper legs, upper arms, and scrotum. Dusky bullae on bilateral dorsal aspect of hands, fingers, toes, and heels. Oral cavity showed 1 violaceous macule on right buccal mucosa and few linear, horizontal, white lines on left buccal mucosa.

Diagnostic Tests:
- Laboratory tests: White blood cell count of 25,600/μL (reference range, 3700-10,500/μL), platelet count of 12,400/μL (reference range, 15,000-40,000/μL). Negative results for herpes simplex virus/varicella zoster virus PCR, syphilis IgG, tissue aerobic culture, fungal culture, and acid-fast bacillus cultures. Positive enterovirus PCR from skin lesion and blood sample.- Pathology:   - Tzanck smear from initial lesion on right dorsal third finger: Negative for multinucleated giant cells  - Punch biopsy from anterior thigh: Showed superficial spongiotic dermatitis, superficial epidermal dyskeratotic necrosis, and mixed acute and chronic inflammation with erythrocyte extravasation  - Direct immunofluorescence: No marking for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, or fibrinogen within epidermis, along dermoepidermal junction, or around dermal vessels- Images:  Image Title: Clinical presentation of skin lesions  Image Description: Patient with numerous erythematous macules, vesicles, and bullae    Image Title: Histopathology of punch biopsy  Image Description: Punch biopsy specimen showing superficial spongiotic dermatitis, superficial epidermal dyskeratotic necrosis, and mixed acute and chronic inflammation with erythrocyte extravasation
